knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Partial Fractions

question.:question/worked-solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{12 x + 12}{(x - 3)(x + 5)} &= \frac{12 x + 12}{(x - 3)(x + 5)}=\frac{A}{x - 3}+\frac{B}{x + 5}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
12 x + 12=A(x + 5)+B(x - 3)
$$

Plugging in $x=-5,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-48 &= -8B \\ B &= 6\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=3,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}48 &= 8A \\ A &= 6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{12 x + 12}{(x - 3)(x + 5)}=\frac{6}{x + 5} + \frac{6}{x - 3}
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }\frac{12 x + 12}{(x - 3)(x + 5)}\,\text{d}x &= \int (\frac{6}{x + 5} + \frac{6}{x - 3})\,\text{d}x \\ &= 6\ln|x - 3|+6\ln|x + 5|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6\ln|x - 3|+6\ln|x + 5|+C &= 1\ln|\left(x - 3\right)^{6} \left(x + 5\right)^{6}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{7}\frac{12 x + 12}{(x - 3)(x + 5)}\,\text{d}x &= [6\ln|x - 3|+6\ln|x + 5|]_{4}^{7} \\ &= (6 \ln{\left(4 \right)} + 6 \ln{\left(12 \right)})-(6 \ln{\left(9 \right)}) \\ &= - 12 \ln{\left(3 \right)} + 12 \ln{\left(2 \right)} + 6 \ln{\left(12 \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3 x + 3}{(x)(x + 3)} &= \frac{3 x + 3}{(x)(x + 3)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x + 3}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
3 x + 3=A(x + 3)+B(x)
$$

Plugging in $x=-3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 &= -3B \\ B &= 2\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=0,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3 &= 3A \\ A &= 1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{3 x + 3}{(x)(x + 3)}=\frac{2}{x + 3} + \frac{1}{x}
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }\frac{3 x + 3}{(x)(x + 3)}\,\text{d}x &= \int (\frac{2}{x + 3} + \frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\ &= 1\ln|x|+2\ln|x + 3|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1\ln|x|+2\ln|x + 3|+C &= 1\ln|x \left(x + 3\right)^{2}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{-1}\frac{3 x + 3}{(x)(x + 3)}\,\text{d}x &= [1\ln|x|+2\ln|x + 3|]_{-2}^{-1} \\ &= (2 \ln{\left(2 \right)})-(\ln{\left(2 \right)}) \\ &= \ln{\left(2 \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Previously, we found that 

$$
\frac{5 x - 10}{(x + 3)(x + 1)}=\frac{25}{2 \left(x + 3\right)} - \frac{15}{2 \left(x + 1\right)}
$$

Now, we can integrate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }\frac{5 x - 10}{(x + 3)(x + 1)}\,\text{d}x &= \int (\frac{25}{2 \left(x + 3\right)} - \frac{15}{2 \left(x + 1\right)})\,\text{d}x \\ &= \frac{25}{2}\ln|x + 3|-\frac{15}{2}\ln|x + 1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{25}{2}\ln|x + 3|-\frac{15}{2}\ln|x + 1|+C &= \frac{1}{2}\ln|\frac{\left(x + 3\right)^{25}}{\left(x + 1\right)^{15}}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-5}^{-4}\frac{5 x - 10}{(x + 3)(x + 1)}\,\text{d}x &= [\frac{25}{2}\ln|x + 3|-\frac{15}{2}\ln|x + 1|]_{-5}^{-4} \\ &= (- \frac{15 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2})-(- \frac{15 \ln{\left(4 \right)}}{2} + \frac{25 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2}) \\ &= - \frac{15 \ln{\left(3 \right)}}{2} + \frac{5 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We'll work out the indefinite integral first and then proceed with the definite integral.

First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4 x + 4}{(x)(x + 3)} &= \frac{4 x + 4}{(x)(x + 3)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x + 3}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
4 x + 4=A(x + 3)+B(x)
$$

Plugging in $x=-3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 &= -3B \\ B &= \frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=0,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4 &= 3A \\ A &= \frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{4 x + 4}{(x)(x + 3)}=\frac{8}{3 \left(x + 3\right)} + \frac{4}{3 x}
$$

Now, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }\frac{4 x + 4}{(x)(x + 3)}\,\text{d}x &= \int (\frac{8}{3 \left(x + 3\right)} + \frac{4}{3 x})\,\text{d}x \\ &= \frac{4}{3}\ln|x|+\frac{8}{3}\ln|x + 3|+C\end{aligned}
$$

We can simplify the result using the laws of logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3}\ln|x|+\frac{8}{3}\ln|x + 3|+C &= \frac{1}{3}\ln|x^{4} \left(x + 3\right)^{8}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{-1}\frac{4 x + 4}{(x)(x + 3)}\,\text{d}x &= [\frac{4}{3}\ln|x|+\frac{8}{3}\ln|x + 3|]_{-2}^{-1} \\ &= (\frac{8 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{3})-(\frac{4 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{3}) \\ &= \frac{4 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3}\ln|x|+\frac{10}{3}\ln|x + 3|+C &= \frac{1}{3}\ln|x^{5} \left(x + 3\right)^{10}|+C\end{aligned}

Finally, the definite integral is 

$$
